<reason>Both sides executed well and honored the format (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure). The decisive clash was CON's dilemma: "expectation" is either a social norm (redundant) or a formal gate (backfires). PRO escaped it in B4.1-B4.2 by arguing that CON's own mechanism—workplaces, schools, and ballots teaching the language—IS expectation at work, so CON was "only fighting the word," and that formal tools' real content is refusing to make remaining outside costless (no indefinite translation subsidies). CON's rejoinder ("naming adds a gate") never engaged that specific content; PRO's translation-subsidy mechanism went unanswered. CON also conceded under B3.1 pressure that large-scale language demands are "just politics," which PRO leveraged into the effective "one-way deal" closing frame. CON's strengths—naturalization evidence, the Amish/Quebec cases, strong Finland/Belgium answers, and superior rhetoric ("theatre," "conscript opportunity and call it a demand")—kept it competitive, but PRO did the cleaner job of defending the motion as written and answering the central "what does it add" burden. Narrow, clear win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The B4.1-B4.2 escape from CON's redundancy/gate dilemma: PRO reframed CON's opportunity mechanism as expectation itself ("CON has conceded the proposition's content and is only fighting the word") and gave expectation concrete content—refusing to subsidize indefinite exit—which CON never squarely neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
